title: "Paired means and alignment"

For ordinary paired-mean inference, one first forms within-pair differences and then performs one-sample inference on those values. The UCCA question is different: it concerns absolute agreement of graph-derived Scene counts, so the focal statistic is a mean absolute difference.

Signed differences answer a directional question: does one language side tend to contain more Scenes? Absolute differences answer an agreement question: how far apart are the paired counts regardless of direction? The absolute value prevents positive and negative differences from canceling, but it also discards direction. Thus the statistic cannot by itself say which language side tends to have the larger count.

The central distinction is between a sampling distribution for independent pairs
and a descriptive permutation of alignments that were never randomly assigned.
The UCCA example uses the first derivation to clarify the estimator and the second
calculation only to show what source-passage matching contributes.

## The general paired-mean result

An estimator is a random function of the sample before observation; its realized
value is an estimate of a fixed target. The [estimator-properties
page](properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables) develops this
distinction.

For signed differences $D_i=Y_{i,A}-Y_{i,B}$, the target and estimator are

$$
\mu_D=\mathbb{E}[D]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\overline D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nD_i.
$$

The within-pair subtraction preserves the pairing: in general,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[D_i]
=\operatorname{Var}[Y_{i,A}]+\operatorname{Var}[Y_{i,B}]
-2\operatorname{Cov}[Y_{i,A},Y_{i,B}],
$$

where [covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd#definition)
measures whether the two centered measurements vary together. The following
reference then assumes that the differences from distinct pairs are
[independent](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent),
while measurements within a pair may remain dependent. With an appropriate t
reference,

$$
\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1},
$$

which yields

$$
\overline D\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{S_D}{\sqrt n}.
$$

This derivation remains useful, but it is not the analysis we impose on the UCCA alignment. The source passages are consecutive literary material rather than randomly sampled translation units, and the paper's agreement question is not a zero signed-mean test.

## The aligned agreement statistic

For source-order pair $i$, let $S_{i,\mathrm{en}}$ and $S_{i,\mathrm{fr}}$ denote Scene counts. Define

$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{aligned}}
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left|S_{i,\mathrm{fr}}-S_{i,\mathrm{en}}\right|.
$$

```{r}
#| label: ucca-aligned-difference
library(ggplot2)

ucca <- read.csv(
  "data/ucca-french-english/passage-counts.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
english <- ucca[ucca$language == "en", ]
french <- ucca[ucca$language == "fr", ]
english <- english[order(english$pair_id), ]
french <- french[order(french$pair_id), ]
stopifnot(identical(english$pair_id, french$pair_id))

pairs <- data.frame(
  pair_id = english$pair_id,
  english_scenes = english$scene_count,
  french_scenes = french$scene_count,
  english_terminals = english$terminal_count,
  french_terminals = french$terminal_count,
  english_words = english$word_count,
  french_words = french$word_count
)
pairs$absolute_difference <- abs(pairs$french_scenes - pairs$english_scenes)
pairs$english_word_rate <- 100 * pairs$english_scenes / pairs$english_words
pairs$french_word_rate <- 100 * pairs$french_scenes / pairs$french_words
pairs$english_terminal_rate <- 100 * pairs$english_scenes / pairs$english_terminals
pairs$french_terminal_rate <- 100 * pairs$french_scenes / pairs$french_terminals

delta_aligned <- mean(pairs$absolute_difference)
word_rate_delta_aligned <- mean(abs(
  pairs$french_word_rate - pairs$english_word_rate
))
terminal_rate_delta_aligned <- mean(abs(
  pairs$french_terminal_rate - pairs$english_terminal_rate
))
stopifnot(abs(delta_aligned - 320 / 154) < 1e-12)

data.frame(
  pairs = nrow(pairs),
  mean_absolute_scene_difference = delta_aligned,
  mean_absolute_difference_per_100_words = word_rate_delta_aligned,
  sensitivity_per_100_terminals = terminal_rate_delta_aligned
)
```

The aligned passages differ by `r sprintf("%.3f", delta_aligned)` Scenes on average.

The code-to-formula mapping is direct: subtraction forms $S_{i,\mathrm{fr}}-S_{i,\mathrm{en}}$, `abs()` removes direction, and `mean()` gives $\Delta_{\mathrm{aligned}}$. The primary rate calculation repeats the same operation after dividing each count by its passage's non-punctuation `word_count`, as defined in the [UCCA exposure dossier](paired-observations.qmd#ucca-exposure-dossier). The terminal-based value checks how much the result changes when punctuation-bearing Layer-0 terminals also enter the denominator.

## A descriptive re-pairing reference

To show what the alignment contributes, we hold the English counts fixed and randomly permute the French passage order. Each draw measures how far arbitrary cross-language pairings lie apart.

```{r}
#| label: ucca-repairing
set.seed(20261018)
re_pairings <- 9999L
repaired_delta <- replicate(
  re_pairings,
  mean(abs(sample(pairs$french_scenes) - pairs$english_scenes))
)
lower_tail_fraction <-
  (1 + sum(repaired_delta <= delta_aligned)) / (re_pairings + 1)

stopifnot(abs(lower_tail_fraction - 0.0001) < 1e-12)

data.frame(
  aligned_difference = delta_aligned,
  mean_repaired_difference = mean(repaired_delta),
  minimum_repaired_difference = min(repaired_delta),
  maximum_repaired_difference = max(repaired_delta),
  descriptive_lower_tail_fraction = lower_tail_fraction
)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-ucca-repairing
#| fig-cap: "Mean absolute Scene-count differences after arbitrary re-pairing. The line is the source-order aligned value."
ggplot(data.frame(mean_absolute_difference = repaired_delta),
       aes(mean_absolute_difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = delta_aligned, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Mean absolute Scene-count difference after re-pairing",
       y = "Re-pairings") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The re-paired mean is `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(repaired_delta))` Scenes, and the plus-one lower-tail fraction is `r format(lower_tail_fraction, scientific = FALSE)`. Each permutation holds both languages' Scene counts fixed and replaces source-passage alignment with an arbitrary one-to-one matching. The fraction therefore reports how often those arbitrary matchings produce a mean absolute difference no larger than the source-aligned value.

Translation alignment was established by the corpus construction rather than by random assignment. The permutations consequently describe the contribution of source matching; they do not reproduce a treatment-assignment process under a sharp null. And because the calculation conditions on the 154 v2 passage pairs, its agreement claim concerns those graphs. Extending that claim to languages, genres, or translators would require a sampling design that represents those broader populations.

## Recap and forward link

1. Absolute differences measure disagreement but remove its direction.
2. Source alignment supplies the defensible pairs.
3. Arbitrary re-pairing is descriptive because translation alignment was not randomized.
4. Word-count normalization checks whether count disagreement mainly reflects different amounts of non-punctuation lexical material; terminal-count normalization is the sensitivity analysis.

The [independent-means page](independent-means.qmd#welchs-standard-error) returns to disjoint speaker groups, where no pairing covariance is available.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does the focal statistic use absolute rather than signed differences?
2. What feature changes across re-pairings?
3. Why is the lower-tail fraction not a randomization-test p value?
4. Why is the per-word rate primary, and what changes in the per-terminal sensitivity calculation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Absolute differences measure passage-level count disagreement without allowing positive and negative signed differences to cancel. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The French Scene counts are assigned to different English passages while each language's marginal counts remain fixed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Translation alignment was not randomly assigned, so permutation does not represent a randomized treatment assignment under a sharp null. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The per-word rate uses non-punctuation Layer-0 nodes as lexical exposure. The sensitivity calculation also counts punctuation terminals, so it asks whether that broader denominator changes the cross-language disagreement. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
